title: Incremental Output Adaptor PRD Notes
content:
Purpose and context:

This doc captures a lightweight PRD sketch for an "Incremental Output Adaptor" layer on the Hosted API. Goal: give application developers a predictable, ergonomic way to consume partially-complete model responses (token-level streaming), integrate deterministic tool handshakes, and receive structured payloads without forcing heavyweight parsing or fragile heuristics client-side. This is intended as a product/SDK-facing change with minimal server-side contract additions and backwards-compatible behavior for existing clients.

Why now:
- Customers building real-time assistants and UIs want sub-200ms first-byte latency and deterministic tool invocation points.
- Many apps need structured atomic events (e.g., action:open_url or action:search) emitted mid-response.
- SDKs today duplicate parsing logic and have brittle heuristics for detecting tool boundaries and JSON blobs in generated text.

Problem statement:
- Streaming gives raw token flows, but lacks a small, explicit handshake for tools and structured outputs.
- Developers must either: parse tokens client-side with regex/heuristics (error-prone), buffer until completion (adds latency), or embed brittle delimiters in prompts (hard to generalize).
- SDK ergonomics are inconsistent across languages: some expose low-level event streams, others provide only final text.

Draft goals (success criteria):
1) Functional: Clients can receive partial, well-typed events (text-chunk, tool-invocation, structured-object) with ordering guarantees and optional replay semantics.
2) Latency: Median first-byte latency <= current streaming baseline; no extra roundtrips required to get structured events.
3) Ergonomics: SDKs provide simple high-level handlers (onText, onToolCall, onObject) plus a low-level raw event stream. 80% of customers can implement common patterns with <= 5 lines of code.
4) Compatibility: Existing non-updated clients continue to receive token streams unchanged.

Non-goals:
- Replacing the model-side tool-calling spec — keep compatibility with existing function-calling semantics.
- Large server-side orchestration for multi-turn tool flows in this initial ship. Focus on deterministic single-invocation events and structured fragments.

Design principles:
- Minimal new wire protocol: embed a concise event framing layer on top of existing streaming SSE/websocket responses.
- Explicit event types with small JSON headers (separate from model-generated JSON payloads) to avoid ambiguity.
- SDKs handle event parsing and provide typed callbacks; fallback to raw tokens for unknown event types.
- Backpressure-friendly: clients can signal small-window (low-latency) mode vs high-throughput mode.

Event model (high-level)
- StreamEvent: one-line JSON header followed by a payload chunk. Types: TEXT_CHUNK, TOOL_CALL_START, TOOL_CALL_PAYLOAD, TOOL_CALL_END, STRUCTURED_EMIT, HEARTBEAT, END_OF_RESPONSE.
- Ordering guarantee: event headers are ordered and delivered in the same sequence the model output was produced.
- Payloads: can be plain text (for TEXT_CHUNK) or opaque bytes/JSON for STRUCTURED_EMIT / TOOL_CALL_PAYLOAD.

Wire example (SSE-like pseudostream):
- data: {"t":"TEXT_CHUNK","id":"c1","meta":{}}
- data: <utf8 bytes containing text for this chunk>
- data: {"t":"STRUCTURED_EMIT","id":"s1","schema":"action.v1"}
- data: {"payload": {"action":"open_url","url":"https://..."}}
- data: {"t":"END_OF_RESPONSE"}

Notes: the header line is always a JSON object indicating event type and metadata; the following data frames contain the event payload. This mirrors patterns used in other streaming APIs but keeps a small explicit separator between header and payload.

Structured output and schema handling:
- Provide a small registry of recommended schema ids (action.v1, table.v1, trace.v1) and encourage model producers to emit the schema id with the STRUCTURED_EMIT event.
- SDKs will include light validators for common schemas and offer typed deserialization hooks.
- For unknown schemas, SDKs expose raw payload and a helper to register custom parsers at runtime.

Tool calling handshake:
- TOOL_CALL_START: header includes tool name and invocation id. This signals the client that the model intends to call a tool.
- TOOL_CALL_PAYLOAD: one or more payload frames containing the arguments (JSON).
- TOOL_CALL_END: final header with status (e.g., sync|async|no-op).
- Server should not execute tools on behalf of the user in-hosted mode by default; this flow is for client-side or middleware handling. Hosted API can optionally wire server-side tool adapters via an explicit opt-in.

SDK ergonomics (sketch):
- Top-level SDK methods: generateStream(request, handlers) -> returns streamHandle.
- Handlers: onText(chunk, meta), onStructured(schemaId, object, meta), onToolCall(startMeta), onToolPayload(invocationId, chunk), onToolEnd(invocationId, resultMeta), onError(err), onDone(meta).
- Example minimal JS usage:
  const stream = client.generateStream({prompt}, {
    onText: (t)=>appendToUI(t),
    onStructured: (schema,obj)=>handleAction(obj),
    onToolCall: (meta)=>{ // show tool UI, or call backend
       showToolPrompt(meta.toolName);
    }
  });

- Safety: SDKs will surface a convenience method to auto-acknowledge TOOL_CALL_START and collect payloads into a single JSON object for synchronous tool invocation. If the app chooses auto-exec, explicit developer opt-in is required.

Backwards compatibility and rollout:
- Default stream behavior for existing clients remains unchanged: they get raw token frames. The new header framing is opt-in via a request flag stream_adaptor=true or via a header Accept: application/x-redwood-adaptor+json.
- Gradual rollout plan: beta opt-in for selected customers -> wider SDK releases -> server default once stability metrics are met.

Metrics and SLOs to track:
- Correctness: percent of STRUCTURED_EMIT events accepted/parsed by SDKs without developer-provided parser. Target >= 90% for recommended schemas.
- Latency: time-to-first-text-byte vs baseline. Target no regression >5%.
- Developer friction: time-to-first-integration (qualitative), number of support tickets mentioning parsing/fragility.

Open questions and risks:
- How to represent partial structured objects? (emit incremental STRUCTURED_EMIT fragments vs buffer until object complete). Proposal: allow TOOL_CALL_PAYLOAD/STRUCTURED_EMIT_PAYLOAD chunking, and expose a progressive parser in SDKs.
- Schema/versioning: need a lightweight governance and deprecations model.
- Security: ensure that structured payloads don't enable unexpected command execution when apps auto-exec. Default to safe sandboxed helpers and require explicit opt-in.

Next steps (short timeline):
- Week 0-2: Align on minimal wire headers and sample SSE payloads with infra and serving runtime.
- Week 2-4: Prototype Node and Python SDK parsers and high-level handlers. Ship internal beta to Solutions Eng for testing.
- Week 4-8: Dogfood with 2 customers building assistant UI and one internal sample app. Collect metrics.
- Week 8-12: Iterate and prepare broader SDK releases and docs/playbooks for migration.

Appendix: sketch of example use-cases
- Real-time agent UI: display streaming text while also showing actions that can be executed mid-response (open links, run search, call payment flow).
- Low-latency monitoring: structured trace events emitted mid-response to update live observability dashboards without waiting for end-of-response.
- Orchestrated tool middleware: middleware receives TOOL_CALL_START and decides whether to execute a server-side tool adapter or prompt the end-user.

This is a working draft. Feedback welcome: what event types are missing, what SDK ergonomics feel awkward, and which schemas should we standardize first?
